newsitem.title: UK: United demands free Heathrow slots from BA.
newsitem.headline: United demands free Heathrow slots from BA.

text.p: United Airlines said on Thursday it was urging Britain's competition authorities to ban British Airways and American Airlines from selling the runway slots they have been asked to give up at London's Heathrow airport as a condition for approving their alliance.

United said in a statement it would be telling the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) today that other airlines should not have to pay for slots needed "to ensure that the proposed alliance between British Airways and American Airlines does not stifle competition and harm consumers in both the United States and the United Kingdom."
United said: "BA and American rather than the competing airlines, must pay the economic price for reducing competition in key markets."

The airline was responding to a request made last month by the OFT for the industry to comment on the conditions British trade minister Ian Lang has proposed for approving the BA and American deal in Britain.

United and other U.S. airlines say the proposals do not go far enough and more slots must be made avalaible as well as ground facilities at Heathrow if BA and American are to be prevented from dominating the transatlantic market.

United said it was proposing to the OFT that BA and American should hand over sufficient slots to allow the introduction of 15 new daily transatlantic flights by other airlines -- equivalent to 210 weekly takeoff and landing slots.
United also said that BA and American should not be allowed to cooperate on London routes to New York, Chicago, Miami and Dallas where they would remain dominant.

Under the proposed alliance BA intends to coordinate its 244 flights a week from Britain to 22 U.S. destinations with all of American's 238 flights a week from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.

BA and American have argued that their deal will lead to greater competition because it will only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. agree "open skies" allowing all U.S. airlines access to Heathrow, the world's busiest international airport and the most popular of all of Europe's transatlantic landfalls.

Under the current aviation agreement dating back to March 1991 only British Airways, Virgin Atlantic Airways, American and United are allowed to use Heathrow for transatlantic services, and their frequencies and routes are restricted.

Rivals say that Heathrow is so crowded that open access would be meaningless unless they were also granted some of British Airways' share of Heathrow's slots, which currently amount to 38 percent and would increase to 42 percent under the alliance with American.
BA says it is prepared to take "reasonable steps" to assist new transatlantic competition at Heathrow and if it had to relase any slots it would have to be done "at a fair market value."
